claims.text: Designerly knowing names an orientation to understanding and changing situations through constructive proposals, modelling and material judgement.
claims.evidenceKind: Historical disciplinary argument and conceptual reasoning model.
claims.qualification: Attribute Cross's three-culture comparison to its educational and disciplinary purpose; he calls it a crude model on p 221.
claims.tension: Scientific and humanities inquiry also construct, model, interpret and intervene. The sources do not establish sealed intellectual cultures or a uniquely designer brain.
claims.confidence: High for the attributed orientation; limited as an exclusive classification of human knowing.

claims.text: Designing can involve proposing both a possible outcome and a working principle that might achieve something valued, then examining their consequences.

evidence.locator: §§2–3, especially Abduction-1/Abduction-2 and the subsequent deduction account

claims.evidenceKind: Conceptual model with illustrative application; inspected publisher section text.
claims.qualification: This is Dorst's constructive account of abduction. Design also uses deduction, induction and other reasoning; not all abduction is identical to this formulation.
claims.tension: A frame can make a proposal coherent without demonstrating that its values are shared or its effects will occur.
claims.confidence: High for Dorst's model; moderate for transfer to a particular inquiry.

claims.text: Practical knowing may be enacted before it is fully described; reflecting on a surprising result can alter how a practitioner understands and acts in the situation.
claims.evidenceKind: Reflective professional epistemology developed through interpreted practice cases.
claims.qualification: The observer's description of knowing-in-action is a reconstruction: Schön explicitly treats it as a theory about knowing, not access to the practitioner's mental contents.
claims.tension: Verbal explanation may contribute to reflection and scrutiny. The claim does not make inarticulacy a mark of superior knowledge.
claims.confidence: High for the source argument and its interpretive limit; moderate transfer.

claims.text: A design frame selects what matters, what counts as a problem and what moves seem worth trying; moves can then revise the frame.
claims.evidenceKind: Conceptual account and interpreted architectural studio episode.
claims.qualification: Frame, action and reflection are mutually related, not a mandatory sequence to be imposed on every project.
claims.tension: A compelling new frame can obscure concerns that fall outside it. Who is authorised to frame the situation remains a separate political question.
claims.confidence: High for the proposed relationship; moderate transfer beyond the illustrated settings.

claims.text: Problem formulations and possible solutions can develop together rather than being completely specified in advance.
claims.evidenceKind: Think-aloud laboratory study of nine experienced industrial designers; outcome ratings by five designer-teachers.
claims.qualification: A 2.5-hour train-litter assignment supports a bounded account of co-evolution, not a universal stage model. The authors credit earlier work by Maher and colleagues.
claims.tension: The study does not compare co-evolution with a randomised linear-method condition, or prove that it invariably improves outcomes. Felt originality also differs from historical novelty.
claims.confidence: High for the observed and interpreted cases; moderate for broader recurrence; limited for comparative effectiveness.

claims.text: A sketch can help someone notice relationships and implications that were not fully formulated before drawing it.

evidence.locator: official CHI short paper, “Experimental Design,” “Method of Analysis,” “Results” and “Conclusions.”

claims.evidenceKind: Retrospective protocol study: two architects and seven advanced students designing an art museum for about 45 minutes.
claims.qualification: Evidence combines drawings, recorded activity and participants' later verbal accounts. It supports the epistemic use of sketches, not the claim that images alone disclose thought.
claims.tension: Retrospective explanations may reconstruct experience; the study has no condition establishing sketching as necessary or always superior.
claims.confidence: High for the bounded study; moderate transfer to other material representations.

claims.text: Material or simulated success can inform inquiry without confirming that a proposal will work in the world.
claims.evidenceKind: Philosophical/practice analysis plus an illustrative full-size mock-up example.
claims.qualification: Schön distinguishes affirmation of a successful move from confirmation of a causal theory; virtual worlds may omit material, cost and other constraints. Mock-ups make some consequences available while withholding others.
claims.tension: The same simplification that permits exploration can hide the consequential resistance of implementation. Additional testing must match the effects claimed.
claims.confidence: High for the distinction; no general effectiveness inference.

claims.text: In contested public situations, deciding what ought to change cannot be separated from disagreement over values and desirable futures.
claims.evidenceKind: Planning-theory argument, supplemented by reflective-practice analysis.
claims.qualification: The Rittel/Webber warrant here is the inspected abstract, not a claimed full-text reading. Apply to contested social-policy settings; not every design problem is wicked.
claims.tension: Plural values do not make evidence or evaluation pointless. Neither a designer's preferred frame nor a workshop majority settles the public good.
claims.confidence: High for the authors' stated position; limited for detailed use of uninspected Rittel passages.

claims.text: Generative design research arranges conditions in which affected people can explore experience and possible futures to inform and inspire design.
claims.evidenceKind: Methodological/practice synthesis and attributed field-positioning model.
claims.qualification: This is the Sanders/Stappers lineage's account. Its landscape is a heuristic, and its term “design research” is narrower than the whole research field.
claims.tension: Providing a toolkit alone does not establish a research question, appropriate participation, a defensible interpretation or a contribution.
claims.confidence: High for this lineage; not an exhaustive definition of all design inquiry.

claims.text: Co-creation, co-design, participatory design and generative research overlap but name different commitments and activities.
claims.evidenceKind: Conceptual distinctions and practice-based historical positioning.
claims.qualification: In SS08, co-creation concerns shared creativity; co-design locates collective creativity within designing. Participants' experiential expertise does not make everyone a professional designer.
claims.tension: Terminology varies across traditions. A neat glossary must not conceal differences in who controls the agenda, analysis or implementation.
claims.confidence: High for the attributed distinctions; moderate as cross-field terminology.

claims.text: Opening design opportunities and evaluating an intervention's effects are different research purposes, even when they interact in one project.
claims.evidenceKind: Methodological framework and practice guidance.
claims.qualification: Treat generative/evaluative as a purpose distinction, not pure phases or a prohibition on evaluation during exploration.
claims.tension: A generative contribution does not exempt an accompanying claim of benefit, learning or empowerment from appropriate outcome evidence.
claims.confidence: High for the distinction; no claim that the purposes are always separable in practice.

claims.text: Saying, doing and making offer complementary, partly overlapping ways of investigating experience.
claims.evidenceKind: Methodological synthesis with a small empirical illustration.
claims.qualification: Interviews can develop unexpectedly; making can be observed and discussed. The sources support combining modes, not assigning each a fixed level of truth.
claims.tension: Observation is interpreted too, and making may be difficult or uncomfortable. No inspected comparison establishes a universal hierarchy with making at the top.
claims.confidence: High for complementarity; limited for comparative superiority.

claims.text: Making a representation can require choices and make aspects of an idea available for inspection, discussion or enactment.
claims.evidenceKind: Methodological argument and illustrative examples.
claims.qualification: Material form enables particular judgements, such as bodily scale or relationships among elements; it does not make every relevant consequence visible.
claims.tension: Available materials and task instructions shape which choices are possible. A polished artefact may conceal uncertainty as readily as expose it.
claims.confidence: High for the proposed mechanism; moderate for its operation in a new setting.

claims.text: Tacit knowing, unrecognised needs, observable conduct and imagined future possibilities should not be treated as interchangeable kinds of hidden content.
claims.evidenceKind: Comparison of authors' conceptual categories and their own account of interpretation.
claims.qualification: “Latent knowledge” in the book and “latent needs” in contextmapping are not identical formulations or settled general epistemological categories. The iceberg is an attributed heuristic, not a measurement.
claims.tension: Difficult speech can also reflect language, anxiety, setting or confidentiality. This is an analytical caution, not a diagnosis of particular participants.
claims.confidence: High for the terminological tension; no warrant for a detector of hidden truth.

claims.text: Sensitising can support attention, recall and reflection over time before a group session, while also changing what becomes salient in that session.
claims.evidenceKind: Methodological account and practice-derived rationale; intervention implication is synthesis.
claims.qualification: Describe actual diaries, prompts, photographs, time demands and uptake. Contextmapping sensitising primarily prepares subsequent work; it is not necessarily the principal data source.
claims.tension: Directed attention is not an untouched baseline, and non-completion or burden can change participation. The book's contested elderly-word priming example is unnecessary to this claim.
claims.confidence: High for documented purposes; moderate for effectiveness; high for the need to disclose shaping.

claims.text: A generative toolkit enables expression partly by constraining it: its images, words, forms and instructions make some associations easier than others.
claims.evidenceKind: Practice-based methodological guidance.
claims.qualification: Report abstraction, tone, cultural fit, component range and any deliberately loaded idea. Open recombination is compatible with finite components.
claims.tension: More choice is not automatically more freedom: too many components or whole magazines can burden or distract participants; highly finished materials can discourage alteration.
claims.confidence: High for the documented design considerations; moderate transfer.

claims.text: Probe-inspired materials can serve different epistemic aims; inspiration through ambiguity is not the same as analysing participant accounts.
claims.evidenceKind: Explicit methodological disagreement, illustrated by probe and contextmapping practices.
claims.qualification: Gaver and colleagues deliberately preserve uncertain returns and do not ask participants to explain them; contextmapping recommends linked accounts for analysis. Neither can stand in for the other's evidence contract.
claims.tension: Recasting every probe as data extraction erases the first approach; treating analytical claims as exempt from explanation misuses its openness. State which contribution is intended.
claims.confidence: High for this substantive disagreement; not a judgement that one approach is universally better.

claims.text: A provotype can use a concrete alternative to expose assumptions or tensions in current practice.

evidence.locator: manuscript pp14–17, especially the travel-registration example on p16

claims.evidenceKind: Conceptual/practice-based argument using activity theory and systems-development examples.
claims.qualification: Use the verified 1992 source and its purpose, not “provotype” as a synonym for any strange prototype. It need not be a preferred future solution.
claims.tension: Provocation may fail, reproduce the designer's assumptions or impose discomfort. The inspected examples establish a rationale and possibility, not universal efficacy.
claims.confidence: High for the rationale and example; moderate transfer.

claims.text: Moving from individual expression into group work transforms what can be said and retained; a collective artefact is not a simple sum of individual views.
claims.evidenceKind: Methodological guidance, programme interpretation and explicit analytical synthesis.
claims.qualification: Accounts may be narrated, challenged, selected, merged or dropped. Keep individual traces and dissent where the study permits them to be connected.
claims.tension: Shared material may help negotiation, but its existence alone does not establish agreement, equal authorship or what absent people would think.
claims.confidence: High for the documented risks; moderate for any particular transformation without its interactional record.

claims.text: Making together can create occasions for exchange without resolving disagreement into a single shared vision.
claims.evidenceKind: Practice guidance, retrospective programme interpretation and a prospective instruction.
claims.qualification: The planning instruction and later account pull in different directions. Disagreement alone does not establish an intended success.
claims.tension: The planning instruction and later account pull in different directions. Disagreement alone does not establish an intended success.
claims.confidence: High for the textual distinction and tension; limited for interaction-level conclusions.

claims.text: Facilitation is part of the inquiry's conditions: prompts, order, silence, time and group composition influence whose contributions become available.
claims.evidenceKind: Methodological guidance and implementation plan.
claims.qualification: Report consequential interventions and roles rather than treating them as invisible logistics. The deliverable requires separate facilitation and data-collection work.
claims.tension: Facilitation can make participation possible while also directing it. Neither the presence nor absence of a facilitator guarantees freedom or reliable interpretation.
claims.confidence: High for the operational considerations; moderate for specific influence absent event evidence.

claims.text: Calling participants experts in their experience is a participatory commitment; it does not by itself equalise authority over framing, interpretation or decisions.
claims.evidenceKind: Conceptual/practice argument with internal tension; analytical synthesis.
claims.qualification: Distinguish expressive opportunity from control of recruitment, funding, ownership and implementation. Schön's reflective contract permits clients to challenge expert judgements.
claims.tension: The book's same-playing-field aspiration is stronger than its evidence. Expertise can be respected while decisions remain structurally unequal.
claims.confidence: High for the distinction; no measured claim that equality was achieved or absent in a specific case.

claims.text: For an analytical use of generative material, an artefact needs to remain linked to its maker's account and circumstances of production.
claims.evidenceKind: Practice-based analytical guidance.
claims.qualification: For this analytical purpose, the prompt, circumstances and relevant interaction matter, as does the connection between photograph and account. An object is not self-interpreting.
claims.tension: This is an analytical requirement suited to the declared aim, not a correction imposed on deliberately unexplained cultural probes; see C17.

claims.text: Data selection and interpretation actively construct an account of the inquiry; they do not simply uncover a meaning already contained in a photograph or collage.
claims.evidenceKind: Methodological and epistemological argument.
claims.qualification: Making can transform meaning, and abstraction loses detail. Name the analyst, unit of attention and interpretive move.
claims.tension: Constructed interpretation need not be arbitrary: returns to the material, alternative readings and explicit warrants allow it to be challenged.
claims.confidence: High for the sources' interpretive position; no claim that all interpretations are equally good.

claims.text: A defensible analytical trail can connect a prompt and situated event to an artefact/account, selected evidence, interpretation, pattern and proposed opportunity.
claims.evidenceKind: Editorial synthesis of documented provenance and analysis practices.
claims.qualification: This chain is a proposed synthesis, not a universal protocol copied from the book. Preserve losses, alternative readings and missing links.
claims.tension: A database or sequence diagram cannot establish rigour by itself; it can faithfully record weak sampling or overinterpretation.
claims.confidence: High for the cited practices; moderate for this proposed combined framework.

claims.text: Analysis becomes more inspectable when observations, interpretations, implications and design ideas are distinguished.
claims.evidenceKind: Methodological guidance.
claims.qualification: Analyst identities, supporting accounts, unplaced material and dated idea histories make interpretation traceable. Intuitive leaps remain proposals for examination.
claims.tension: Neat categories do not eliminate judgement or preconceptions. Disagreement and material that resists the themes should remain visible.
claims.confidence: High for the recommended practice; no guarantee of validity from procedural compliance.

claims.text: Comparing people, methods and data forms can challenge and reformulate an interpretation as well as corroborate it.
claims.evidenceKind: Methodological argument about iterative comparison and triangulation.
claims.qualification: Agreement among related sources can arise from shared prompts, assumptions or participants; report dependencies rather than counting agreement as independent confirmation.
claims.tension: Contradictions may expose different contexts or meanings rather than an error to average away. Triangulation does not turn interpretations into objective facts automatically.
claims.confidence: High for the source's account; moderate for the strength of any resulting claim.

claims.text: A proposed future is an interpretive and imaginative outcome, not a prediction of behaviour or an inevitable consequence of the data.
claims.evidenceKind: Methodological argument and bounded qualitative thematic study.
claims.qualification: Separate what participants imagined, what analysts synthesised and what designers later proposed. Stated preferences and narrated futures remain situated expressions.
claims.tension: A compelling possibility may be unrealistic, contested or weakly supported as a policy choice. Further inquiry is needed for feasibility, uptake and effects.
claims.confidence: High for the status distinction; limited for prediction.

claims.text: Design inspiration and a publicly defensible research claim can require different forms of accountability.
claims.evidenceKind: Practice methodology and proposed research-through-design evaluation framework.
claims.qualification: Immersion may be useful without yielding explicit generalised conclusions. RTD07 proposes process, invention, relevance and extensibility as evaluation lenses, not a universally validated checklist.
claims.tension: Practical learning need not become academic research to matter. Conversely, usefulness to a designer does not establish a general claim about people or institutions.
claims.confidence: High for the distinction and framework attribution.

claims.text: Research through design contains a live disagreement about how knowledge should accumulate; rigorous documentation need not imply a single convergent theory.

evidence.locator: accepted manuscript, “Theory from Research Through Design,” convergence discussion and annotated-portfolio proposal, PDF pp3–9

claims.evidenceKind: Philosophical/methodological debate, not an effectiveness experiment.
claims.qualification: Gaver argues for provisional, contingent and aspirational accounts and annotated portfolios; he still asks for clearer conceptual and methodological articulation.
claims.tension: Plurality does not exempt claimed effects from evidence. The two positions should be shown as a tension rather than retrospectively reconciled into one universal method.
claims.confidence: High for the inspected arguments; limited as a verdict on the whole field.

claims.text: Producing an intelligible new frame is different from securing institutional acceptance or the capacity to act on it.

evidence.locator: “Cases and Methods,” “Research Process,” “Reframing Dialogues” and “Discussion” (including its limitations paragraphs)

claims.evidenceKind: Qualitative study of two university–government projects; separate programme participant-evaluation evidence.
claims.qualification: Lee's Singapore collaborations involved students and motivated public-sector partners; the tactics are situated. Democracy Labs participants' requests for follow-through are a different body of evidence, not a replication of Lee.
claims.tension: Reframing may unsettle a mandate or exceed an institution's capabilities. A change in conversation is not evidence of implemented change.
claims.confidence: High for the documented distinction; moderate transfer; limited for downstream outcomes.

claims.text: Claims about “creativity” need a stated meaning and evidence appropriate to that meaning.
claims.evidenceKind: Structured review of a selected HCI literature corpus with coding.
claims.qualification: The review narrowed 998 keyword records to a citation-weighted, pre-2016 coded set of 208 papers. Coding agreement was limited on the reported subset; the corpus is neither all creativity research nor current HCI.
claims.tension: Frequent tool-building, laboratory studies or collaboration in that corpus do not establish that a tool or collaboration reliably makes people more creative.
claims.confidence: High for the review's scope and reported concerns; limited for universal creativity claims.

claims.text: The value of design practice cannot be established by displaying a familiar workshop sequence; making, craft and attention to context matter to the claim being made.
claims.evidenceKind: Practitioner critical essay plus methodological guidance.
claims.qualification: Kolko criticises simplified design-thinking practices but also sees value in wider strategic adoption. His essay is not a systematic comparison of training or workshop outcomes.
claims.tension: Avoid both promotional certainty and blanket dismissal. A familiar process can be useful, but its label supplies no evidence of research quality or benefit.
claims.confidence: High for the authors' positions; limited for claims of comparative effectiveness.

claims.text: The Democracy Labs toolkit documents designed conditions and intended data collection; it does not itself demonstrate their enactment or success.
claims.evidenceKind: Prospective public deliverable and later interpretive programme chapter.
claims.qualification: Targets such as 180 participants are plans, not achieved counts. The deliverable explicitly permits deviations and does not present a controlled experiment. Its prompts include substantive democratic and utopian assumptions.
claims.tension: A later output that echoes a prompt is not necessarily spontaneous preference. The chapter's account of conditions is not proof that each planned condition operated as intended.
claims.confidence: High for the documented plan and declared chapter scope; limited for enactment without linked records.

claims.text: The programme publications examine different corpora, so their claims must not be merged into a single participant-level chain of evidence.
claims.evidenceKind: Cross-publication scope audit of empirical and interpretive reports.
claims.qualification: The imaginaries paper analyses individual pre-workshop material from five cities, excluding collective outputs; the evaluation analyses 103 survey responses and 26 interviews; the chapter describes six-country work with 161 participants. These are scope descriptors, not reconstructed identities.
claims.tension: Related publications and shared programme participants do not provide independent replication. Anonymous booklets cannot be connected to demographics or later voices without evidence permitting that link.
claims.confidence: High for reported corpus differences; limited for their overlap, which remains unresolved.

claims.text: The reported citizens' imaginaries illuminate possibilities expressed in particular recruited urban European settings, not the preferences of citizens in general.
claims.evidenceKind: Qualitative analysis of questionnaires and anonymous booklet material.
claims.qualification: Recruitment varied by city; diversity efforts do not establish representativeness. The study analysed selected booklet pages and questionnaire material, with translation and researcher coding.
claims.tension: Self-selection and absent non-participants may exclude important orientations. Positive, negative and minority views of experts, technology and participation should not disappear in a single optimistic narrative.
claims.confidence: High for the bounded thematic account; limited for prevalence or population generalisation.

claims.text: Positive reports of voice, listening and respect indicate how responding participants experienced the Labs, while leaving lasting empowerment and institutional effects open.
claims.evidenceKind: Post-event questionnaire and voluntary video-interview evaluation; no pre/post or control design.
claims.qualification: Reports were collected 1–10 days later. Nonresponse, device access, education and willingness to be filmed constrain the account. Self-reported confidence is not a measured causal change in agency.
claims.tension: Some participants questioned sensitising, confidence gains, dominance or future follow-through. The chapter's categorical “fully met” conclusion exceeds the mixed evidence it reports.
claims.confidence: High for the presence of positive and critical self-reports; limited for causal or durable empowerment claims.

claims.text: A credible account should preserve friction and inconsistencies rather than making every difficulty a confirmation of the method.
claims.evidenceKind: Critical comparison of related reports; editorial inference.
claims.qualification: For example, the chapter's all-booklets-returned account and the article's non-return/non-completion account need scope reconciliation. Some numerical and prose/table inconsistencies remain in the reports.
claims.tension: Friction can reveal something and still indicate burden or a method limitation. Institutional horizons may be an analytical finding and a constraint on what the inquiry could generate.
claims.confidence: High for the existence of textual tensions; limited for their explanation pending original records.

claims.text: Communicating an inquiry is another transformation: selection, anonymisation and presentation can change what an account means and how credible it appears.
claims.evidenceKind: Communication methodology, reporting choices and public protocol
claims.qualification: Preserve artefact-account relationships, translations and selections, and distinguish participant expression from editorial interpretation. Public anonymity can remove meaningful context.
claims.tension: Transparency does not mean unrestricted disclosure. A vivid identifiable quotation or image can be rhetorically powerful while exceeding the available permission or misrepresenting its setting.
claims.confidence: High for the methodological and document boundaries; no claim about any person's actual consent.

claims.text: The protocol distinguishes participation, recording and permission to publish identifiable media.
claims.evidenceKind: Public methodological protocol
claims.qualification: The public protocol does not establish which permission a particular person gave. This is a distinction in the records, not a legal determination.
claims.tension: Publication of a research report does not clear every underlying photograph or recording.
claims.confidence: Direct for the published protocol; no inference about executed permissions

claims.text: The INCITE-DEM Labs explored democratic participation procedures and possible futures in six European settings.
claims.qualification: They were not representative national parliaments or trials of implemented policy.

claims.text: The case encompasses consortium design, situated encounters, and later interpretation and translation.
claims.qualification: The five levels in this inquiry are analytical organisation, not five empirically separable causal stages.

claims.text: Lamas and colleagues foreground designed conditions through which democratic concerns become articulable and negotiable.
claims.qualification: This is a conceptual account, not causal proof or direct mapping of thought.

claims.text: Consortium co-design reportedly took about six months across several disciplines.
claims.qualification: No complete version history or citizen control of this upstream design is shown.

claims.text: The protocol targeted about 180 participants, suggesting 30 per site and different commitments for citizens, stakeholders and policymakers.
claims.qualification: Target is not attendance; role categories do not erase overlapping identities.

claims.text: D4.3 reports 161 people across Trondheim, Rome, Lisbon, Potsdam, Barcelona and Ljubljana.
claims.qualification: The report says recruited; other sources say engaged or attended. The underlying attendance register was not inspected.

claims.text: Individual and evaluation papers cover five cities and use different response corpora.
claims.qualification: The 143 recruits or attendees, 128 questionnaires, 113 reported booklets, 103 evaluation responses and 26 interviews do not form one longitudinal dataset.

claims.text: Recruitment differed by site, including company/database, registry invitations and public outreach.
claims.qualification: Purposive diversity and stratification attempts do not establish population representativeness.

claims.text: Lisbon recruitment used vouchers and personal contact, yet three early recruits dropped out after preparation.
claims.qualification: The reasons remain uncertain. The account does not establish intimidation, burden or vulnerability as the cause.

claims.text: An accessible venue, quiet movable furniture, materials, refreshments and staffing were explicit design conditions.
claims.qualification: Requirements do not prove each venue complied or that barriers were removed.

claims.text: The protocol planned two and a half hours of preparation across ten working days, followed by two workshop days for most participants.
claims.qualification: This is a planned total, not a daily requirement or measured effort. The booklet assigns 30 minutes to the questionnaire, compared with 40 in the protocol.

claims.text: Registration, information, consent and continuing facilitator contact preceded the workshop.
claims.qualification: Forms and general reports are not executed consent evidence for each person.

claims.text: Booklets invited accounts of past and recent experiences, both encouraging and frustrating, alongside feelings and possible changes.
claims.qualification: Prompted articulation is not an untouched baseline or exhaustive recovery of tacit knowledge.

claims.text: A questionnaire about an ideal democracy in 2050 structured individual imagination, including questions about exclusion.
claims.qualification: Its optimistic, better-than-today framing shapes expression. It is not neutral preference polling.

claims.text: Simulation was included in the planned preparation and described as optional in the early Lisbon account.
claims.qualification: No universal use or learning effect can be inferred.

claims.text: Local-language responses were translated into English for programme analysis.
claims.qualification: A complete record from original response to translation, and equivalence of meaning, have not been independently established.

claims.text: Shared material could connect experience to provisional group framing.
claims.qualification: A shared canvas is not unanimous agreement; time and abstraction caused difficulty.

claims.text: Mapping compared experienced and desired democratic principles in Lisbon.
claims.qualification: It is situated appraisal, not measured quality of national democracy.

claims.text: Provotyping used a masked planning case to provoke critique and alternative processes.
claims.qualification: The exercise was not a vote on the actual case and does not establish later political action.

claims.text: Lisbon groups disagreed about timing of participation: five preferred early involvement, one later after expert studies.
claims.qualification: These are distinct group outputs, not a population preference distribution or evidence of every member's agreement.

claims.text: Futuring used fictional utopian news and unlimited-resource invitations.
claims.qualification: The environment is normatively framed; outcomes should not be labelled wholly spontaneous.

claims.text: Wheels, stories and enactment made proposals more specified and discussable.
claims.qualification: Specification is not feasibility or benefit; the epistemic explanation is an argued inference.

claims.text: The protocol asks for consensual understanding, while the later chapter distinguishes coordination and layered imaginaries.
claims.qualification: Without group interaction evidence, convergence cannot be declared either absent or achieved.

claims.text: The protocol assigned facilitation and data collection separately. Country teams also translated and adapted materials.
claims.qualification: The staffing plan is not a census of actual workers. Facilitation can both enable and direct contributions.

claims.text: The project reports a multimodal corpus of recordings, notes and artefacts.
claims.qualification: Reports of existence do not make the complete corpus publicly inspectable.

claims.text: The sources do not establish that everyone returned or completed the booklet.
claims.qualification: Different scopes may contribute but do not themselves explain the contradiction.

claims.text: Individual-imaginaries analysis used selected booklet questions and questionnaire material, excluding collective output.
claims.qualification: Neither all booklet pages nor every visual/embodied contribution was analysed in this paper.

claims.text: The article reports 939 coded extracts, 101 codes and seven questionnaire themes, alongside a separate booklet analysis.
claims.qualification: Frequencies are coded-material proportions, not population percentages or policy votes.

claims.text: Translation, response consolidation, segmentation, coding and theme construction transform the material.
claims.qualification: Changes or losses of context are possible consequences of these transformations, not proof that every translation was poor.

claims.text: The inspected public workbook contains 128 questionnaire responses and 112 booklet rows.
claims.qualification: The article and workbook overview report 113 booklets. The difference remains unresolved; the deposited count is not a corrected article total.

claims.text: The deposited data provide no common identity key linking questionnaires, booklets, workshops and evaluation.
claims.qualification: Similar wording or demographics cannot establish same-person continuity.

claims.text: A Barcelona booklet expression about quiet voices appears under inclusive/respectful dialogue in the article.
claims.qualification: The article's B8 label identifies a published passage. It is not a demographic profile or group identifier.

claims.text: A Potsdam questionnaire response imagines a chair for nature and absent interests.
claims.qualification: This is an imagined element, not a physical chair observed in the Lab.

claims.text: A Potsdam response connects neighbourhood experience and barriers of time and money to a paid Democracy Day.

evidence.locator: single Potsdam questionnaire response, minimised paraphrase

claims.qualification: No verified identity link connects this response with the later Potsdam group proposal.

claims.text: The public data diagnose discrepancies in the article's education table and some quotation identifiers.

evidence.locator: response categories and published/deposited text correspondence

claims.qualification: The sources contain count and identifier discrepancies. This inquiry does not supply a corrected demographic distribution or a universal identity crosswalk.

claims.text: D4.3 consolidates 31 group proposals with city and group identifiers.
claims.qualification: Group identifiers permit bounded group traces, not person-level origins. Titles vary between prose accounts and later publications.

claims.text: Lisbon group 6 describes its Houses of Citizenship proposal through a service network and a fictional school-transport story.
claims.qualification: The mother and child are fictional characters. Their story is neither a participant biography nor an implemented service.

claims.text: Barcelona group 4's reported experience critique and food-system proposal can be followed within a named group.
claims.qualification: The source does not show intermediate turns proving the critique caused the proposal.

claims.text: Cross-country innovation analysis interprets 31 innovations and identifies a subset of 13 oriented to post-growth.
claims.qualification: This is an analyst classification of prompted proposals, not 13 implemented transitions or a majority public preference.

claims.text: The later interpretation identifies existing institutional horizons and combinations of incremental and more ambitious changes.
claims.qualification: Calling friction productive cannot rule out limitations of the method or the time available.

claims.text: Evaluation respondents often valued voice, listening, respect and group work.
claims.qualification: Nonresponse, self-selection, the absence of a baseline or control group, and conflicting scores limit generalisation.

claims.text: Preparation was not useful for a substantial minority, despite the methodological rationale.
claims.qualification: Usefulness and ease are different questions. Neither universal rejection nor universal benefit is established.

claims.text: Some respondents reported dominance, shyness or wanting less speech.
claims.qualification: The reports answer different questions in small groups. Their percentages cannot simply be added, and they do not establish that officials caused the difficulties.

claims.text: Participants questioned technical demands, utopian distance, follow-through and policymakers' roles.
claims.qualification: Minority comments identify tensions, not prevalence or a controlled comparison.

claims.text: The evaluation does not establish lasting empowerment or dismantled social hierarchy.
claims.qualification: Positive self-reports are meaningful but narrower than strong author conclusions.

claims.text: Researchers selected 20 of 31 imaginaries for the fora according to institutional fit, transferability and discussability.
claims.qualification: Selection exercises authority. Excluded examples include moneyless society and clean-energy island.

claims.text: The selected 20 were merged into 6 models and rewritten as stories.
claims.qualification: These are authored consolidations; complete proposal-by-proposal membership is not exposed.

claims.text: Nine fora between June and September 2025 engaged 106 participants from policy, administration and non-governmental organisations.
claims.qualification: Target 135 was not reached. Recruitment and cancellations shape whose institutional judgement is available.

claims.text: The fora discussed strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, threats, possible adaptations and anticipated effects.
claims.qualification: The discussion design supports claims about appraisal and anticipated effects, rather than observed impact.

claims.text: Institutional actors raised resource, legal/administrative, inclusion, technological and integration concerns.

evidence.locator: executive synthesis pp8-9 and model responses

claims.qualification: Their expectations are not observed future effects or vetoes enacted in policy.

claims.text: The case documents reception and translation but no complete named proposal-to-adoption-to-impact chain.
claims.qualification: The inspected reports document reception and further development. Their lack of a complete adoption chain does not establish that nothing happened elsewhere.

claims.text: The original plan for four final films developed into a game and six fictional futures.
claims.qualification: An evolution of public communication, not failure inferred solely from departure from plan.

claims.text: D4.4 reports trials, playtests, feedback and refinement of the later game.
claims.qualification: Small situated tests do not establish transferable learning effects or durable civic participation.

claims.text: D4.4's six futures and D5.2's six models are different output sets.
claims.qualification: Their equal number and related themes do not make the fictional futures and institutional models interchangeable.

claims.text: The participant-to-researcher-to-institutional-audience route changes authority and communicative purpose.
claims.qualification: This is an analytical account, not a quantified estimate of redistributed power.

claims.text: The protocol distinguishes research access, recording and public media use.
claims.qualification: The protocol is not a participant-specific publication permission.

claims.text: The questionnaire and assessment form have openly licensed public records. Original explanatory diagrams can make the inquiry inspectable without republishing participant media.
claims.qualification: The public licences apply to the identified records, not automatically to participant media or every project output.

claims.text: The case supports situated articulation, interpretation, speculative proposal and methodological learning.
claims.qualification: It does not establish latent-truth extraction, representativeness, universal method superiority or political impact.

claims.text: The inspected records contain count, identifier and reporting discrepancies that limit particular claims.
claims.qualification: Missing links remain unresolved even when the available records can be presented together.

claims.text: Returning results and inviting participant feedback were promised in the protocol.
claims.qualification: Delivery, participant response and its influence are not verified for the full cohort.

claims.text: A selected Rome participant account connects the booklet with becoming familiar with the method and arriving more relaxed.
claims.qualification: No identifier links this account to a specific booklet, group, storyboard or later evaluation. Rome's collective activities are a separate event-level account.

claims.text: The provotype combined the Fuglmyra planning case, document review and professional/citizen interviews into a masked narrative; timelines and presentations were later thematically interpreted.
claims.qualification: A designed representation of a case; no complete contribution-to-code-to-concept audit trail. Not all conceptual-prototype features are verbatim participant proposals.

claims.text: Norwegian participant contact led to a small follow-up workshop; a separate workshop with five municipal professionals supplied criticism that changed the neighbourhood-centre concept.
claims.qualification: The citizen workshop count conflicts: the table reports seven, including five original participants, while the prose reports six. Both workshops are dated 28 May 2024. Their order, complete feature revisions and subsequent adoption remain unverified.

claims.text: Lisbon used the Norwegian case for distance/comparability, yet groups introduced local land/metro examples; at least one group experienced dominating members.
claims.qualification: The claimed benefits of a foreign case are organiser interpretations. Local historical examples are participant accounts, not independently verified events. The identities behind the dominance report are unavailable.

claims.text: D5.1 separately analyses provotyping speech through coding and co-occurrence, and questionnaire text through eight topics generated with latent Dirichlet allocation.
claims.qualification: Topic probabilities are not population beliefs, and co-occurrence is not causation. The reported 31 provotype narratives conflict with 36 listed narratives; the survey count of 132 also differs from other versions.

claims.text: D5.3 examines appeal and expected effectiveness through online vignette and conjoint tasks in seven countries.
claims.qualification: The study uses hypothetical choices with panel, age, quota and screening constraints, and reports inconsistent final sample counts. It does not establish field implementation or validate all 31 proposals.

claims.text: Democracy Allowance's monthly paid leave stimulus received divergent responses: Barcelona sought accredited hours, Tallinn more frequent participation, and other fora raised cost/monitoring concerns.
claims.qualification: Forum participants are not representative national opinion; no determination of legal feasibility or evidence that a government adopted the model.

claims.text: The final roadmap recommends civic leave with nationally determined frequency and compensation decoupled from salary, plus neighbourhood participation infrastructure.
claims.qualification: The changed specification is visible against D52, but no formal change-log attributes it to a particular forum comment. Pilots, funding and legal recognition are recommendations.

claims.text: Later fiction trials reportedly involved 253 participants; the game was formatively tested with eight people in two sessions, leading to specific rule/card revisions.
claims.qualification: The 253 participants are not a demonstrated continuation of the original Lab cohort. The game sample was small, with no measured durable learning or civic effect. Fiction-trial instructions differ on whether participants encountered three or six stories.

claims.text: Common structures were adapted locally, including recruitment, grouping, officials' attendance and session timing.
claims.qualification: Event dates and publication dates are distinct. Country labels do not explain outcomes causally. Potsdam's exact event date remains unverified in the inspected records.

claims.text: Lamas and colleagues use programme theory, infrastructuring and activity theory to interpret the designed conditions.
claims.qualification: These are complementary lenses in their account, not three independently tested mechanisms or a neutral measurement model.

claims.text: The protocol promises restricted access, withdrawal, institutional storage, separate public-image permission and end-project destruction of personal data.
claims.qualification: Commitments distinguish personal data from retained research outputs. No operational compliance, destruction or withdrawal audit was possible; translated outputs alone prove neither compliance nor violation.

claims.text: D5.3 reports aggregate preference for citizen-only rather than all-resident eligibility in hypothetical forums.
claims.qualification: This is a preference under the instrument, not proof of real exclusion decisions, a universal national position or respondents' underlying motives.

claims.text: An early Lisbon account reports a participant describing being heard, her ideas being adopted, and later reflection on the value of her experience.
claims.qualification: The adopted idea and her booklet are unidentified. The report does not establish lasting empowerment.
claims.confidence: Bounded retrospective report selected by the source authors

claims.text: The current Democracy Labs site distributes workshop templates and describes an adaptable facilitation sequence.

evidence.locator: Core Toolkit Materials and All-in-one Download

claims.qualification: Current public guidance and file availability do not establish how every original Lab operated or what later use achieved.
claims.confidence: Direct for the published account; bounded for enactment or consequences

claims.text: The toolkit page reports that students adapted it to design and facilitate a participatory workshop.
claims.qualification: This is a bounded report of reuse. The page does not establish sustained adoption, comparative learning effects or political consequences.
claims.confidence: Direct for the published account; bounded for enactment or consequences

claims.text: The game page describes Lab material informing six fictions and their trials, then game development and playtesting. The published rules ask players to agree on a proposal.
claims.qualification: This supplies a programme-reported development route and intended rule. It does not map each contribution to each card or establish durable effects.
claims.confidence: Direct for the published account; bounded for enactment or consequences

claims.text: The Barcelona policy-dialogue report describes discussion of nine draft recommendations, including feasibility, inclusion, clarity and feedback.

evidence.locator: From ideas to refinement and Key insights from group deliberations

claims.qualification: The report documents consultation about recommendations, not adoption. Its nine draft recommendations are not interchangeable with the final roadmap version, and no allowance-specific revision log is supplied.
claims.confidence: Direct for the published account; bounded for enactment or consequences

site.title: Designerly Ways of Knowing
site.standfirst: How can proposing, making and reflecting help people understand a situation while trying to change it? Explore design as inquiry, generative research as an arranged encounter, and Democracy Labs as a case with visible evidence and limits.

modeDescriptions.presentation: Follow the argument from material moves to generative inquiry, interpretation and limits.
modeDescriptions.explore: Follow relations among concepts, questions and tensions.
modeDescriptions.labs: Inspect how contributions and proposals changed across encounters, research and institutional reception.

site.landingCardCopy: How proposing, making and reflecting contribute to inquiry, and how generative research turns situated expression into contestable interpretations and possibilities.
site.evidenceNote: This inquiry uses a bounded set of inspected records. An unverified link is not proof that nothing happened beyond those records.

concepts.label: Designerly ways of knowing
concepts.definition: An orientation to finding out through framing, constructive proposals, representation and situated judgement. Cross argued that these practices deserve a place in general education.
concepts.tension: Other fields also construct, imagine and intervene. Distinctiveness need not mean exclusivity.

evidence.locator: §§2–3, especially Abduction-1/Abduction-2 and the subsequent deduction account

caseLinks.bridge: The Citizenship House story makes a proposed arrangement inspectable; it does not establish a uniquely designer form of cognition.

concepts.interpretiveStatus: Attributed account or working synthesis; read the linked claim qualifications

concepts.label: Inquiry and intervention
concepts.definition: Inquiry seeks understanding; intervention changes conditions. A design move can do both, while leaving its wider effects untested.
concepts.tension: Learning from an intervention differs from demonstrating its benefit.

evidence.locator: “Cases and Methods,” “Research Process,” “Reframing Dialogues” and “Discussion” (including its limitations paragraphs)

caseLinks.bridge: Norwegian follow-up reportedly changed a concept. That continuation does not establish a functioning municipal service.

concepts.interpretiveStatus: Attributed account or working synthesis; read the linked claim qualifications

concepts.label: Research and design research
concepts.definition: Research articulates a contribution whose question, procedure, interpretation and limits can be examined. Design research can study design, inform designing or contribute through designing.
concepts.tension: Practical learning matters without automatically becoming a public research claim.

evidence.locator: accepted manuscript, “Theory from Research Through Design,” convergence discussion and annotated-portfolio proposal, PDF pp3–9

caseLinks.bridge: The booklet passage becomes evidence through a stated analytical selection, rather than through its existence alone.

concepts.interpretiveStatus: Attributed account or working synthesis; read the linked claim qualifications

concepts.label: Generative design research
concepts.definition: In the Sanders, Stappers and Sleeswijk Visser lineage, generative research arranges encounters through which people explore experience and possibilities to inform design.
concepts.tension: A toolkit does not supply the whole research design or equalise authority.

caseLinks.bridge: Preparation, materials and the collective setting belong to the inquiry, although this participant's later artefact is unlinked.

concepts.interpretiveStatus: Attributed account or working synthesis; read the linked claim qualifications

concepts.label: Research through design
concepts.definition: Designing and its artefacts can materially contribute to a research argument. Accounts differ on how such knowledge should accumulate and be assessed.
concepts.tension: Zimmerman's assessment lenses and Gaver's provisional accounts remain different methodological positions.

evidence.locator: accepted manuscript, “Theory from Research Through Design,” convergence discussion and annotated-portfolio proposal, PDF pp3–9

caseLinks.bridge: The evolving neighbourhood-centre concept invites questions about a design contribution. The case is not relabelled an agreed example of every research-through-design approach.

concepts.interpretiveStatus: Attributed account or working synthesis; read the linked claim qualifications

concepts.label: Ill-defined and wicked problems
concepts.definition: An ill-defined problem lacks a settled formulation. Wicked problems add a stronger planning argument about contested ends and public values.
concepts.tension: Wicked does not mean merely difficult, and not every design problem is wicked.

caseLinks.bridge: Different views of participation timing expose contested purposes. They do not classify every Lab task as wicked.

concepts.interpretiveStatus: Attributed account or working synthesis; read the linked claim qualifications

concepts.label: Framing and reframing
concepts.definition: Framing selects what matters and what actions seem worth trying. Reframing changes those selections in response to difficulty, consequences or another perspective.
concepts.tension: A compelling frame can still exclude concerns or exceed institutional authority.

evidence.locator: “Cases and Methods,” “Research Process,” “Reframing Dialogues” and “Discussion” (including its limitations paragraphs)

caseLinks.bridge: The institutional selection criteria made some proposals eligible for discussion while excluding others.

concepts.interpretiveStatus: Attributed account or working synthesis; read the linked claim qualifications

concepts.label: Problem-solution co-evolution
concepts.definition: Developing a possible response can change the understanding of the problem, which can redirect the response. Dorst and Cross examined this relation in a bounded designer study.
concepts.tension: The study does not establish a mandatory sequence or superiority over all alternatives.

caseLinks.bridge: The reported revision after municipal feedback invites a co-evolution reading; the detailed sequence is insufficient to establish every change of frame.

concepts.interpretiveStatus: Attributed account or working synthesis; read the linked claim qualifications

concepts.label: Constructive abduction
concepts.definition: Dorst describes proposing an arrangement and sometimes its working principle in relation to something valued. The proposal remains conjectural and requires further examination.
concepts.tension: A coherent proposal does not prove shared values or successful effects.

evidence.locator: §§2–3, especially Abduction-1/Abduction-2 and the subsequent deduction account

caseLinks.bridge: The fictional service story specifies actors and connections through which inclusion might be pursued.

concepts.interpretiveStatus: Attributed account or working synthesis; read the linked claim qualifications

concepts.label: Deduction
concepts.definition: A proposed arrangement and working principle allow reasoning about expected consequences. Those conclusions remain conditional on the premises and model.
concepts.tension: A valid implication does not establish that its premises describe the world.

evidence.locator: §§2–3, especially Abduction-1/Abduction-2 and the subsequent deduction account

caseLinks.bridge: Forum responses question a model's expected consequences. They are not a controlled test confirming its predictions.

concepts.interpretiveStatus: Attributed account or working synthesis; read the linked claim qualifications

concepts.label: Induction
