presentation.title: What can we learn by trying to change a situation?
presentation.claim: What can we learn by trying to change a situation?
presentation.copy: A proposed arrangement can make a relationship visible, expose a difficulty or change what seems worth pursuing. Designing can contribute to understanding through this traffic between a question, a move and its consequences. The inquiry begins with that relation.
presentation.visibleQualification: This is a synthesis across accounts of designing, not a claim that every act of making produces research knowledge.
presentation.visualPurpose: Introduce a concrete question-move-consequence relation through a labelled illustrative example, without presenting a universal cycle.
presentation.transition: Any proposed change already contains a judgement about what would be appropriate.
presentation.argumentFunction: Establish the epistemic question before naming methods.
presentation.optionalInteraction: No additional interaction; use the common evidence and concept links.

presentation.title: Appropriate for whom, and under what conditions?
presentation.claim: Appropriate for whom, and under what conditions?
presentation.copy: Design concerns arrangements in a human-made world. Cross emphasised constructive inquiry and judgements of appropriateness. Such judgements join purposes, people and circumstances: an arrangement can serve one group while burdening another. Technical ingenuity does not settle which ends should prevail.
presentation.visibleQualification: Cross's comparison of intellectual cultures is a heuristic. Science and the humanities also construct, interpret and imagine.
presentation.visualPurpose: Place a proposed arrangement beside its purposes, affected people and constraints; show competing judgements without scoring them.
presentation.transition: Before proposing an arrangement, someone has selected what counts as the problem.
presentation.argumentFunction: Explain the object and value-laden character of design.
presentation.optionalInteraction: No additional interaction; use the common evidence and concept links.

presentation.title: A frame selects what matters.
presentation.claim: A frame selects what matters.
presentation.copy: A frame names relevant features, identifies a difficulty and makes some actions seem worth trying. It also leaves things outside the question. Reframing changes those selections. It can follow a surprise, an unsuccessful move or a perspective the initial account overlooked.
presentation.visibleQualification: A persuasive reframe is a proposal about the situation, not discovery of its uniquely correct hidden problem.
presentation.visualPurpose: Show the same illustrative meeting arrangement under access and deliberation frames. Identify what each frame attends to and leaves open.
presentation.transition: Possible responses can then change the problem that a frame makes visible.
presentation.argumentFunction: Make framing and reframing consequential rather than terminological.
presentation.optionalInteraction: No additional interaction; use the common evidence and concept links.

presentation.title: Problems and possible solutions can develop together.
presentation.claim: Problems and possible solutions can develop together.
presentation.copy: A possible response can reveal a new constraint or opportunity. That changes the understanding of the problem, which redirects the next response. Dorst and Cross examined this co-evolution in a study of nine experienced industrial designers working on a bounded task.
presentation.visibleQualification: The study supports an interpreted relationship in that setting. It does not establish a mandatory sequence or prove superiority over every alternative.
presentation.visualPurpose: Use two aligned revision tracks, one for the question and one for the proposal, with labelled cross-influences rather than a seamless loop.
presentation.transition: The reasoning that proposes a possible arrangement remains conjectural.
presentation.argumentFunction: Show reciprocal development, grounded in a bounded empirical study.
presentation.optionalInteraction: No additional interaction; use the common evidence and concept links.

presentation.title: A constructive proposal connects means with something valued.
presentation.claim: A constructive proposal connects means with something valued.
presentation.copy: In Dorst's account, designing may require proposing both an arrangement and a working principle through which it could achieve a valued outcome. This is constructive abduction. Deductions can explore expected consequences, and observations can challenge the proposal. These forms of reasoning work together.
presentation.visibleQualification: A plausible connection is not proof that the value is shared or the effect will occur.
presentation.visualPurpose: Display value, proposed arrangement and proposed working principle as explicit terms, with a separate question about examination.
presentation.transition: Reasoning also occurs through practical activity that may precede a full verbal account.
presentation.argumentFunction: Differentiate constructive conjecture from proof and exclusive reasoning faculties.
presentation.optionalInteraction: No additional interaction; use the common evidence and concept links.

presentation.title: Practical knowing need not begin as a verbal rule.
presentation.claim: Practical knowing need not begin as a verbal rule.
presentation.copy: Schön describes knowing in action: competent judging and adjusting that need not be preceded by an explicit account of how to act. People may later describe aspects of that knowing. The description is a reconstruction, not transparent access to the understanding that directed every move.
presentation.visibleQualification: Being unable to explain an action does not make it more reliable, skilled or true.
presentation.visualPurpose: Contrast an activity record with a later account in two labelled registers; neither is drawn as a deeper layer.
presentation.transition: Unexpected consequences can make practical understanding available for reconsideration.
presentation.argumentFunction: Establish the distinction between practical knowing and its description.
presentation.optionalInteraction: No additional interaction; use the common evidence and concept links.

presentation.title: Reflection can change the next move.
presentation.claim: Reflection can change the next move.
presentation.copy: A situation can surprise a practitioner while action remains possible. Reflection in action questions a judgement, makes another move and attends to what follows. Reflection on action revisits an activity afterward. The distinction concerns the relation to action, not simply fast versus slow thought.
presentation.visibleQualification: A successful move can affirm a direction without confirming the causal explanation attached to it.
presentation.visualPurpose: Annotate the revision tracks with surprise, reconsideration and a changed move; show retrospective reflection as a separate return.
presentation.transition: Representations give this conversation a material form that can be inspected again.
presentation.argumentFunction: Explain reflection in and on action without reducing them to stages.
presentation.optionalInteraction: No additional interaction; use the common evidence and concept links.

presentation.title: Representations can help develop thought.
presentation.claim: Representations can help develop thought.
presentation.copy: A sketch, model or enactment can make a relationship perceptible before it has been fully formulated in words. Making does more than display a finished idea. In Suwa and Tversky's small sketch study, drawings and retrospective accounts together supported analysis of what participants noticed.
presentation.visibleQualification: The evidence does not show that images alone reveal thought or that sketching is always superior to other forms of inquiry.
presentation.visualPurpose: Show a new relation becoming inspectable in a labelled schematic arrangement, paired with an explanatory account.
presentation.transition: What can be learned depends on which consequences the representation makes available.
presentation.argumentFunction: Establish the epistemic contribution of external representation.
presentation.optionalInteraction: No additional interaction; use the common evidence and concept links.

presentation.title: Consequences have a scope.
presentation.claim: Consequences have a scope.
presentation.copy: A relation noticed in a drawing, a difficulty encountered in a mock-up and a change observed in an operating service are different kinds of evidence. Simplification makes exploration manageable. It can also omit costs, institutions, materials and people that matter in practice.
presentation.visibleQualification: Success within a representation or encounter does not by itself establish success in the implemented world.
presentation.visualPurpose: Compare representation, encounter and implementation using repeated fields: what is available, what is omitted and what claim is warranted.
presentation.transition: The same care is needed when describing what a person knows or can express.
presentation.argumentFunction: Prevent an upgrade from model consequence to real-world effectiveness.
presentation.optionalInteraction: No additional interaction; use the common evidence and concept links.

presentation.title: Expression is partial and constructive.
presentation.claim: Expression is partial and constructive.
presentation.copy: The generative literature distinguishes explicit, observable, tacit and latent forms of knowing. These terms are not a settled set of hidden objects. Tacit knowing concerns limits of articulation; latent language may concern needs or future possibilities. A later expression can be developed through the inquiry itself.
presentation.visibleQualification: Making does not establish complete access to a person's tacit knowing or recover a future preference intact.
presentation.visualPurpose: Use a term-comparison table with definitions and non-equivalences. Avoid depth, size or height as a proxy for epistemic value.
presentation.transition: Different expressive modes create complementary opportunities and different interpretive demands.
presentation.argumentFunction: Differentiate knowing, articulation and imagination; reject the depth hierarchy.
presentation.optionalInteraction: No additional interaction; use the common evidence and concept links.

presentation.title: Saying, doing, making, enacting and imagining can inform one another.
presentation.claim: Saying, doing, making, enacting and imagining can inform one another.
presentation.copy: Saying can explain reasons and meanings. Doing shows activity under particular conditions. Making gives a possibility form. Enacting brings bodies, timing and sequence into view. Imagining explores what is absent or not yet experienced. These modes overlap within encounters and often require each other.
presentation.visibleQualification: No mode occupies a higher level of truth. Observation and material form also require interpretation.
presentation.visualPurpose: Compare five modes across invitation, possible contribution and interpretive limit, without arrows of ascent.
presentation.transition: Generative design research deliberately arranges such encounters.
presentation.argumentFunction: Explain complementary epistemic functions before introducing the research family.
presentation.optionalInteraction: No additional interaction; use the common evidence and concept links.

presentation.title: Generative research arranges an inquiry with people.
presentation.claim: Generative research arranges an inquiry with people.
presentation.copy: In the Sanders, Stappers and Sleeswijk Visser lineage, generative design research invites people to explore experience and possible futures to inform design. It includes preparation, encounters, documentation, interpretation and communication. Co-creation names shared creativity; co-design places collective creativity within designing.
presentation.visibleQualification: These terms overlap but are not interchangeable. A workshop or toolkit alone does not establish a research contribution.
presentation.visualPurpose: Place the encounter inside an arrangement of recruitment, prompts, materials, facilitation, documentation and interpretation.
presentation.transition: The encounter often begins before people meet.
presentation.argumentFunction: Locate generative design research within the broader epistemic argument.
presentation.optionalInteraction: No additional interaction; use the common evidence and concept links.

presentation.title: Preparation supports attention and also directs it.
presentation.claim: Preparation supports attention and also directs it.
presentation.copy: Sensitising can give people time to notice, remember and develop accounts before a collective session. Diaries, booklets and short tasks supply prompts and recall cues. They also focus attention and require effort. What later becomes expressible belongs to that history of preparation.
presentation.visibleQualification: This is a methodological rationale, not a law that preparation necessarily produces deeper or more accurate knowledge.
presentation.visualPurpose: Place the invitation, time demand, possible contribution and burden beside each other. A preparation strip ends at an encounter, not at a truth claim.
presentation.transition: Materials within the encounter continue to shape what can be expressed.
presentation.argumentFunction: Explain sensitising as both support and intervention.
presentation.optionalInteraction: No additional interaction; use the common evidence and concept links.

presentation.title: Tools enable expression partly by constraining it.
presentation.claim: Tools enable expression partly by constraining it.
presentation.copy: A finite set of images, words or forms can make it easier to begin and combine ideas. Ambiguity may invite association; incompleteness may invite alteration. Content, abstraction and cultural references still shape the available expression. Too much choice or an inaccessible task can make participation harder.
presentation.visibleQualification: An open invitation is designed. Its usefulness depends on people, purpose and setting.
presentation.visualPurpose: Show two illustrative invitations with different permitted choices. Annotate enabling and constraining effects as hypotheses, not measured participant outcomes.
presentation.transition: Similar materials can serve different research purposes.
presentation.argumentFunction: Explain the epistemic work of toolkit design, ambiguity and incompleteness.
presentation.optionalInteraction: Toggle between two labelled illustrative invitations; retain both as a readable comparison. Do not ask visitors to submit personal material.

presentation.title: A material's purpose changes its evidence contract.
presentation.claim: A material's purpose changes its evidence contract.
presentation.copy: A probe can preserve uncertainty for inspiration. Contextmapping links making and telling for interpretation. A prototype can explore a developing possibility. A provotype can question assumptions in current practice. The same object may serve different purposes in different encounters.
presentation.visibleQualification: Gaver's probe argument and contextmapping's analytical commitments should not be merged into a single method for extracting hidden knowledge.
presentation.visualPurpose: Compare purpose, treatment of returns and warranted contribution across four method families. Make disagreement visible.
presentation.transition: Individual material then changes when other people encounter and work with it.
presentation.argumentFunction: Differentiate methods by epistemic purpose and preserve a substantive dispute.
presentation.optionalInteraction: No additional interaction; use the common evidence and concept links.

presentation.title: Collective work transforms individual contributions.
presentation.claim: Collective work transforms individual contributions.
presentation.copy: An account may be explained, extended, contested, selected or ignored in group work. Shared material can sustain coordination across different views. A completed group artefact records a collective product, but does not reveal every contribution, silence or negotiation that made it possible.
presentation.visibleQualification: Coordination and consensus are different. Shared authorship and unanimous agreement require their own evidence.
presentation.visualPurpose: Track several contributions into a shared object with named operations and an explicitly unrecorded contribution history.
presentation.transition: Who can contribute, and whose interpretation prevails, depends on the arrangement.
presentation.argumentFunction: Explain individual and collective creativity without presuming consensus.
presentation.optionalInteraction: No additional interaction; use the common evidence and concept links.

presentation.title: Participation distributes opportunities and authority unevenly.
presentation.claim: Participation distributes opportunities and authority unevenly.
presentation.copy: Recruitment, language, time, facilitation and materials affect what can be contributed. Researchers may still control questions, categories and circulation. Institutions retain decision powers outside the room. Consent to participate, permission to record and permission for public media use also differ.
presentation.visibleQualification: Being heard respectfully is consequential, but it does not establish equal control over the inquiry or its consequences.
presentation.visualPurpose: Display who contributes, who decides, who receives and who is absent at several movements. Do not use a single participation score.
presentation.transition: These conditions belong in the record used to interpret the material.
presentation.argumentFunction: Make ethics, exclusion and power part of the epistemic argument.
presentation.optionalInteraction: No additional interaction; use the common evidence and concept links.

presentation.title: An artefact needs an account and a context.
presentation.claim: An artefact needs an account and a context.
presentation.copy: For an analytical use of generative material, retain the prompt, circumstances, maker's account and relevant interaction. A photograph alone cannot explain what an arrangement meant. Provenance makes the material's origin recoverable; interpretive traceability connects it to the claim later made.
presentation.visibleQualification: Traceability need not expose private records. It also does not make an interpretation neutral or correct.
presentation.visualPurpose: Place prompt, expression, account and context around a selected analytical claim. Each link names what it supports and what is unavailable.
presentation.transition: Analysis adds further decisions about what to select, compare and say.
presentation.argumentFunction: Explain the evidence object and the conditions of a recoverable interpretation.
presentation.optionalInteraction: No additional interaction; use the common evidence and concept links.

presentation.title: Interpretation is made through accountable judgement.
presentation.claim: Interpretation is made through accountable judgement.
presentation.copy: Researchers select material, segment it, compare instances and construct categories or themes. Those operations change what the material can mean and do. An observation, interpretation, implication and design idea should remain distinguishable so that a reader can examine the move between them.
presentation.visibleQualification: Constructed meaning need not be arbitrary. The question is whether the reading is defensible and open to challenge.
presentation.visualPurpose: Use a transformation ledger with columns for material, operation, actor, resulting claim and limit. No automatic data-to-wisdom funnel.
presentation.transition: An interpretation becomes easier to examine when contrary material remains visible.
presentation.argumentFunction: Explain the movement from traces to interpretations and possibilities.
presentation.optionalInteraction: No additional interaction; use the common evidence and concept links.

presentation.title: Disagreement can change the account.
presentation.claim: Disagreement can change the account.
presentation.copy: Comparing people, methods and records can challenge an interpretation as well as corroborate it. Preserve material that does not fit, distinguish alternative readings and return to the source. Agreement among related records may reflect shared prompts or participants rather than independent confirmation.
presentation.visibleQualification: Triangulation does not turn a claim into objective truth automatically. Contradictions may remain unresolved.
presentation.visualPurpose: Place a proposed reading beside a counterinstance and the narrower claim that survives. Give the counterinstance equal visual weight.
presentation.transition: The kind of contribution being claimed determines what further warrant is needed.
presentation.argumentFunction: Make disagreement and negative cases operational rather than ceremonial.
presentation.optionalInteraction: No additional interaction; use the common evidence and concept links.

presentation.title: A contribution needs a warrant suited to its purpose.
presentation.claim: A contribution needs a warrant suited to its purpose.
presentation.copy: A situated account, reframing, possibility, prototype and claim of effectiveness ask different things of evidence. Research through design contains disagreement about how contributions should accumulate: Zimmerman's assessment lenses and Gaver's provisional, contingent accounts are not one settled standard.
presentation.visibleQualification: Usefulness to a design process does not establish prevalence, causal benefit or institutional impact.
presentation.visualPurpose: Compare contribution, relevant warrant and inference that does not follow. Preserve the research-through-design disagreement as attributed positions.
presentation.transition: Democracy Labs lets us inspect these distinctions across an extended research system.
presentation.argumentFunction: Connect practical learning, research contribution and limits of transfer.
presentation.optionalInteraction: No additional interaction; use the common evidence and concept links.

presentation.title: Democracy Labs designed conditions for democratic inquiry.
presentation.claim: Democracy Labs designed conditions for democratic inquiry.
presentation.copy: Within INCITE-DEM, six European Lab settings invited people to explore participation procedures and possible futures. Citizens worked with facilitators and country teams in a consortium-designed inquiry. Later research, institutional fora and public products transformed the material for different purposes and audiences.
presentation.visibleQualification: The Labs did not themselves enact the institutions imagined. The five levels shown here are an analytical organisation of the case.
presentation.visualPurpose: Orient the reader through five equal-weight levels: encounter, Lab, country, programme and institutional horizon. Show cross-level movements without a progress ladder.
presentation.transition: Begin with what one participant reported, and identify where her trace stops.
presentation.argumentFunction: Provide a strong case orientation before opening detailed examples.
presentation.optionalInteraction: No additional interaction; use the common evidence and concept links.

presentation.title: A reported encounter has a boundary.
presentation.claim: A reported encounter has a boundary.
presentation.copy: A Rome participant described initial apprehension, growing familiarity through the booklet and a more relaxed arrival. The organiser's account also describes the collective work of that Lab. It does not identify her group or artefact. Other evidence reports preparation burdens, dominance and doubts about follow-through.
presentation.visibleQualification: Her account and those criticisms remain separate records. Neither supplies a complete participant biography or a causal measure of empowerment.
presentation.visualPurpose: Trace the reported sequence to arrival, then use a labelled setting connection and a visible break before an unidentified group output.
presentation.transition: A different record permits a more precise expression-to-category trace.
presentation.argumentFunction: Demonstrate participant experience while preserving the identity gap.
presentation.optionalInteraction: No additional interaction; use the common evidence and concept links.

presentation.title: An expression becomes an analytical example.
presentation.claim: An expression becomes an analytical example.
presentation.copy: A Barcelona booklet expression describes respect and listening to quieter voices. The individual-imaginaries article selects it under inclusive and respectful dialogue. English text correspondence links the deposited passage and published example. The category belongs to the researchers' analysis.
presentation.visibleQualification: The available record does not expose the full translation and coding history or connect the passage to a workshop group.
presentation.visualPurpose: Display invitation, minimal paraphrase, researcher category and missing translation or coding detail as distinct objects.
presentation.transition: Making a future story performs another kind of work: it specifies a possibility.
presentation.argumentFunction: Make analytical transformation concrete without implying extraction of a hidden value.
presentation.optionalInteraction: No additional interaction; use the common evidence and concept links.

presentation.title: A fictional character makes a proposal more specific.
presentation.claim: A fictional character makes a proposal more specific.
presentation.copy: In Lisbon's Citizenship House story, a fictional mother seeks school transport for a child with disabilities. The proposed houses would connect people, services and institutions. The story turns a broad concern with inclusion into actors, places, procedures and dependencies that can be discussed.
presentation.visibleQualification: The mother and child are fictional. The account does not establish an operating service, feasibility or benefit.
presentation.visualPurpose: Show the proposed service sequence as conditional steps, with FICTIONAL SCENARIO visible at the beginning and in the text equivalent.
presentation.transition: A group proposal can then acquire a further identity in research analysis.
presentation.argumentFunction: Explain the epistemic work of storymaking without documentary fiction.
presentation.optionalInteraction: No additional interaction; use the common evidence and concept links.

presentation.title: A group identifier supports continuity, not a causal story.
presentation.claim: A group identifier supports continuity, not a causal story.
presentation.copy: Barcelona group 4 reported an account of tenants excluded from an apartment-solar decision. The same published group later produced a Self-managed Food System. Researchers classified that proposal in the cross-country analysis. The group link is documented; the intervening reasoning is not fully available.
presentation.visibleQualification: The earlier account cannot be said to have caused the later proposal. The researchers' classification is not automatically the participants' own label.
presentation.visualPurpose: Separate same-group continuity from researcher classification, with a labelled missing negotiation between the early account and proposal.
presentation.transition: At the institutional boundary, researchers made a further selection and rewrite.
presentation.argumentFunction: Distinguish provenance, causation and analytical categorisation.
presentation.optionalInteraction: No additional interaction; use the common evidence and concept links.

presentation.title: Institutional circulation changes the proposal.
presentation.claim: Institutional circulation changes the proposal.
presentation.copy: Researchers selected 20 of 31 innovations and merged them into six models for institutional fora. Democracy Allowance proposed monthly paid time with unmonitored use. Responses differed over frequency, accreditation, cost and equity. A later roadmap recommended a revised allowance and future pilots.
presentation.visibleQualification: The full proposal-to-model and comment-to-revision histories are unavailable. Reception and recommendation do not establish adoption or effects.
presentation.visualPurpose: Compare selection criteria, model features, contrasting forum responses and later recommendation. Explicit breaks prevent invented item ancestry or causal revision.
presentation.transition: A separate Norwegian continuation shows another route beyond the workshop.
presentation.argumentFunction: Make downstream selection, power and political limits inspectable.
presentation.optionalInteraction: No additional interaction; use the common evidence and concept links.

presentation.title: Inquiry can continue without becoming implementation.
presentation.claim: Inquiry can continue without becoming implementation.
presentation.copy: In Norway, participant contact led to further meetings and a small citizen workshop. A separate workshop with municipal professionals supplied criticism that reportedly changed a neighbourhood-centre concept. This documents continued inquiry and conceptual revision beyond the original Lab.
presentation.visibleQualification: The two workshops share a date, but their order is unknown. Detailed feature changes, municipal adoption and effects are not established.
presentation.visualPurpose: Use partly ordered branches for citizen and municipal feedback, converging on reported conceptual revision. Stop before implementation with a named gap.
presentation.transition: The contribution is clearest when its grounds and its limits stay together.
presentation.argumentFunction: Avoid both a success story and the false conclusion that every idea stopped at the workshop.
presentation.optionalInteraction: No additional interaction; use the common evidence and concept links.

presentation.title: What can this inquiry support?
presentation.claim: What can this inquiry support?
presentation.copy: Designing can make relationships, judgements and possibilities available for understanding. Generative research arranges encounters in which such contributions can develop. Its claims remain answerable to the conditions, material, interpretations and transformations that produced them. A useful possibility can be situated, contestable and unfinished.
presentation.visibleQualification: Neither making, participation nor publication establishes truth, equality or impact by itself.
presentation.visualPurpose: End with three inspectable questions: what became available, under which conditions, and through which interpretive moves. Link each to a concept path and case journey.
presentation.transition: Continue through a question in Explore or follow a concrete journey in Democracy Labs.
presentation.argumentFunction: State the qualified intellectual position and open two purposeful continuations.
presentation.optionalInteraction: Choose 'How did this become evidence?' or 'Who controlled the next transformation?' Both open a named route with context preserved.

case.title: Democracy Labs

orientation.text: Democracy Labs was a generative inquiry within INCITE-DEM into how people might participate in decisions and shape democratic institutions for sustainable futures. Six European Lab settings brought citizens together with facilitators, country teams and some institutional participants.

The inquiry began with preparation and continued through shared work, documentation, analysis and later public or institutional products. The 2024 Labs, the later institutional fora and the later game are different encounters with different participants and purposes.

You can follow selected accounts, expressions, group proposals, classifications and institutional responses. No inspected record joins one participant continuously from preparation to a political effect. Each journey shows what connects and where the evidence stops.

case.deepLinkOrientation: Democracy Labs explored possible participation arrangements. You are inspecting one bounded part of that inquiry.
case.orientationLimit: These five levels organise the evidence. They are not a five-step method or a ranking of certainty.

stakeholders.receives: Receive a shared framework and material for local and cross-country inquiry.
stakeholders.asymmetry: Full translation and adaptation histories are unavailable.

stakeholders.label: Researchers and analysts
stakeholders.contribution: Select, code, compare, interpret and publish material.
stakeholders.authority: Choose units, categories, examples and claims.
stakeholders.receives: Receive research material and opportunities for scholarly contribution.
stakeholders.asymmetry: Experiential expertise does not imply control over the analytical account.

stakeholders.label: Project partners
stakeholders.contribution: Co-design and coordinate the programme and its later products.
stakeholders.authority: Allocate resources and organise divisions of labour and outputs.
stakeholders.receives: Receive deliverables, publications and methodological products.
stakeholders.asymmetry: Programme purposes shape what is made communicable.

stakeholders.label: Public institutions in Labs or local follow-up
stakeholders.contribution: Contribute institutional experience or professional criticism.
stakeholders.authority: Retain formal powers outside the encounter; influence discussion within it.
stakeholders.asymmetry: Original Lab participation and the Norwegian municipal follow-up are different roles and events.

stakeholders.label: Institutional fora participants
stakeholders.contribution: Appraise models and propose adaptations or anticipated consequences.
stakeholders.authority: Judge institutional fit without a demonstrated adoption mandate.
stakeholders.asymmetry: Their responses are neither national opinion nor implementation decisions.

stakeholders.label: Later publics and practitioners
stakeholders.contribution: May read, discuss, play or adapt public products.
stakeholders.authority: Choose whether and how to engage within available resources and permissions.
stakeholders.receives: Receive publications, stories, instruments and a game.
stakeholders.asymmetry: Availability and small playtests do not establish reach, equitable use or durable effects.

stakeholders.label: Absent or non-completing people
stakeholders.contribution: Sometimes leave dropout or non-return traces; other perspectives are unavailable.
stakeholders.authority: No voice is assigned by this reconstruction.
stakeholders.receives: What they received or would have contributed is not established.
stakeholders.asymmetry: Attendees cannot stand for missing perspectives; reasons for absence remain uncertain.

tensions.positionA: Generative methodology uses language of access to tacit or latent knowing.
tensions.positionB: The same methodological literature describes elicitation and active interpretation.
tensions.consequence: Keep the terms attributed and the expression partial; do not depict hidden contents moving intact into an artefact.

tensions.label: Inspiration and analytical accountability
tensions.positionA: Gaver and colleagues preserve uncertainty in probe returns for inspiration.
tensions.positionB: Contextmapping links artefacts and accounts for analytical interpretation.
tensions.consequence: Ask what kind of contribution is intended before judging its evidence contract.

tensions.label: Coordination, consensus and authority
tensions.positionA: Shared materials can support working together across difference.
tensions.positionB: Agreement instructions, dominance and later selection can narrow which differences survive.
tensions.consequence: A shared object cannot certify unanimity or equal authority.

tensions.label: Articulated contribution and methodological plurality
tensions.positionA: Zimmerman and colleagues propose lenses for assessing research-through-design contributions.
tensions.positionB: Gaver challenges convergence toward comprehensive theory and proposes provisional accounts and portfolios.
tensions.consequence: Make contributions inspectable without presenting one universally settled evaluation scheme.

tensions.label: Expressive opportunity and institutional power
tensions.positionA: An encounter can be valued and a proposal can become more discussable.
tensions.positionB: Authority, resources and institutional criteria still govern what can travel or be implemented.
tensions.consequence: Distinguish being heard, shaping a model, receiving a response and changing policy.
